name: Single-Leg Squat on BOSU Ball
description: A single-leg squat performed on the dome of a BOSU ball (dome side up), combining the balance challenge of the unstable dome surface with the unilateral loading of a single-leg squat. This requires simultaneous control of balance, knee alignment, hip stability, and ankle proprioception on an unstable surface. Used in advanced rehabilitation programs and sport-specific balance training for athletes requiring single-leg stability under load.

execution.starting_position: Step onto the center of the BOSU dome with one foot. Lift the other foot off the dome. Establish balance with the eyes open and a wall or bar within reach.
execution.setup_instructions: Master bilateral BOSU squats and single-leg floor squats before combining them. Have a safety surface or partner nearby at all times.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the BOSU dome on one foot. Find balance.
Step 2: Slowly descend into a single-leg squat, allowing the BOSU to respond to the balance shifts.
Step 3: Descend to 60-70 degrees of knee flexion with the knee tracking over the second toe.
Step 4: Drive through the foot to return to standing. Repeat, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you descend. Exhale as you drive up.
common_mistakes: Knee caving inward (valgus) during the descent — drive the knee out over the second toe
Not controlling the BOSU wobble — the ankle must actively manage the instability
Using too deep a squat before the balance and strength are adequate
safety_considerations: ALWAYS have a safety surface within reach — a wall, rack, or partner
Do not attempt without first mastering bilateral BOSU squats and single-leg floor squats
If knee pain occurs during the descent, reduce depth
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: 60-70 degrees of knee flexion is the target initially. Full depth only when balance and strength allow.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric, 1s pause at bottom, 2s concentric return.
coaching_cues: Push the knee out over the second toe — no knee cave
Let the ankle respond to the dome — do not stiffen the ankle to prevent wobble
Focus on a fixed point ahead for balance
